difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE because it rests on one concept (norm preservation is equivalent to A^T A = I) followed by 2-3 short deductions (det A = ±1 for full rank, |λ| = 1 for the eigenvalues) and a counterexample such as the 90-degree rotation to reject (B) and (C); about 2 minutes.
stem: An $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with real entries satisfies the property: $\|Ax\|^2 = \|x\|^2$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, where $\| \cdot \|$ denotes the Euclidean norm. Which of the following statements is/are ALWAYS correct?

options.label: B
options.text: $A = I$, where $I$ denotes the identity matrix, is the only solution

options.label: C
options.text: The eigenvalues of $A$ are either $+1$ or $-1$

solution.quick: $\|Ax\|^2 = \|x\|^2$ for all $x$ means $x^\top (A^\top A - I) x = 0$ for all $x$; as $A^\top A - I$ is symmetric, $A^\top A = I$, so $A$ is orthogonal (A) with $\det A = \pm 1$, hence full rank (D). $-I$ and the $90^\circ$ rotation also satisfy the property, so $I$ is not the only solution (B), and the rotation's eigenvalues are $\pm i$, not $\pm 1$ (C). Answer: **(A), (D)**.

steps.title: Rewrite the norm condition as a quadratic form
steps.body:
For a real vector, $\|v\|^2 = v^\top v$. Hence

$$
\|Ax\|^2 = (Ax)^\top (Ax) = x^\top A^\top A\, x, \qquad \|x\|^2 = x^\top x = x^\top I\, x .
$$

The given property therefore says

$$
x^\top M x = 0 \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}^n, \qquad \text{where } M = A^\top A - I .
$$

Note that $M$ is **symmetric**, because $(A^\top A)^\top = A^\top A$.

steps.title: A symmetric matrix with zero quadratic form is zero, so A is orthogonal
steps.body:
Test the identity on special vectors ($e_i$ is the $i$-th standard basis vector):

- $x = e_i$: $\;e_i^\top M e_i = M_{ii} = 0$ for every $i$.
- $x = e_i + e_j$ ($i \ne j$): $\;M_{ii} + M_{jj} + M_{ij} + M_{ji} = 0 + 0 + 2M_{ij} = 0$, so $M_{ij} = 0$ (using $M_{ij} = M_{ji}$).

So $M = 0$, i.e.

$$
A^\top A = I .
$$

For a square matrix a left inverse is also a right inverse, so $A^{-1} = A^\top$ and $AA^\top = I$ as well. This is exactly the definition of an **orthogonal matrix**: **(A) is correct**. (Conversely, every orthogonal matrix satisfies the property, since $x^\top A^\top A x = x^\top x$.)

For $n = 2$ the check can be done by expanding: with $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$, $\|Ax\|^2 - \|x\|^2 = (a^2 + c^2 - 1)x_1^2 + 2(ab + cd)x_1x_2 + (b^2 + d^2 - 1)x_2^2$, and all three coefficients vanishing is precisely $A^\top A = I$.

steps.title: Full rank (D)
steps.body:
Two quick arguments:

1. **Null space.** If $Ax = 0$ then $\|x\| = \|Ax\| = 0$, so $x = 0$. The null space is $\{0\}$, the nullity is $0$, and by rank–nullity $\operatorname{rank} A = n$.
2. **Determinant.** $\det(A^\top A) = \det(A^\top)\det(A) = (\det A)^2 = \det I = 1$, so $\det A = \pm 1 \ne 0$.

Either way $A$ is invertible, i.e. has full rank: **(D) is correct**.

steps.title: Eigenvalues (C): modulus 1, but not necessarily real
steps.body:
Let $Av = \lambda v$ with $v \ne 0$, where $\lambda$ and $v$ may be complex. Since $A$ is real, $A^* = A^\top$, and

$$
|\lambda|^2\, v^* v = (Av)^*(Av) = v^* A^\top A\, v = v^* v \;\Longrightarrow\; |\lambda| = 1 .
$$

So every eigenvalue lies on the unit circle. A **real** eigenvalue must be $\pm 1$, but complex ones are allowed. Counterexample: the $90^\circ$ rotation

$$
R = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad Rx = \begin{bmatrix} -x_2 \\ x_1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \|Rx\|^2 = x_2^2 + x_1^2 = \|x\|^2 .
$$

Its characteristic polynomial is $\det(R - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 + 1$, so its eigenvalues are $\pm i$, which are neither $+1$ nor $-1$. Hence **(C) is not always correct**. (More generally, a rotation by $\theta$ has eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta}$.)

steps.title: Uniqueness (B) and summary
steps.body:
Many matrices other than $I$ preserve norms: $-I$, the reflection $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, the rotation $R$ above, and in fact every orthogonal matrix. So $A = I$ is **not** the only solution: **(B) is incorrect**.

| Option | Always true? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (A) | Yes | $\|Ax\|^2 = \|x\|^2\ \forall x \iff A^\top A = I$ |
| (B) | No | $-I$, reflections and rotations also work |
| (C) | No | $\lvert\lambda\rvert = 1$, but the $90^\circ$ rotation has $\lambda = \pm i$ |
| (D) | Yes | $\det A = \pm 1 \ne 0$ (equivalently, trivial null space) |

The always-correct statements are **(A), (D)**.

solution.teaching:
**Orthogonal matrices are exactly the length-preserving ones.** A real square matrix $Q$ is *orthogonal* when $Q^\top Q = I$, which says its columns are orthonormal. Then $\|Qx\|^2 = x^\top Q^\top Q x = x^\top x = \|x\|^2$, so $Q$ preserves lengths. This question is about the converse: if lengths are preserved for every $x$, then $x^\top (Q^\top Q - I) x = 0$ for all $x$, and because $Q^\top Q - I$ is symmetric this forces $Q^\top Q = I$. The key fact is that a symmetric matrix is completely determined by its quadratic form (polarization: $x^\top M y = \tfrac14\left[(x+y)^\top M (x+y) - (x-y)^\top M (x-y)\right]$ for symmetric $M$). Preserving lengths also preserves inner products and angles, so orthogonal matrices are the rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that fix the origin: rotations, reflections and their compositions.

**Consequences worth remembering.**

- $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$, so $Q$ is invertible and has full rank $n$.
- $\det Q = \pm 1$, from $(\det Q)^2 = \det(Q^\top Q) = 1$: $+1$ for rotations, $-1$ for reflections.
- Every eigenvalue satisfies $|\lambda| = 1$: it lies on the unit circle in $\mathbb{C}$. Real eigenvalues can only be $\pm 1$, but complex pairs $e^{\pm i\theta}$ appear for rotations by $\theta$.
- All singular values equal $1$.

**Why the eigenvalue claim fails.** A $90^\circ$ rotation of the plane moves every nonzero vector off its own line, so it has no real eigenvector at all; its characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 + 1$ has roots $\pm i$. The statement "eigenvalues are $\pm 1$" holds only for special orthogonal matrices, for example symmetric ones such as reflections: $Q = Q^\top = Q^{-1}$ gives $Q^2 = I$, so $\lambda^2 = 1$.

**Back to this question.** The condition $\|Ax\|^2 = \|x\|^2$ for all $x$ is exactly $A^\top A = I$, so $A$ is orthogonal (A) and invertible, hence of full rank (D). Many orthogonal matrices other than $I$ exist ($-I$, reflections, rotations), which rules out (B), and rotations have non-real eigenvalues, which rules out (C). Answer: **(A), (D)**.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\|Ax\|^2 = \|x\|^2$ means $x^\top (A^\top A - I) x = 0$ for all $x$. Since $A^\top A - I$ is symmetric, it must be the zero matrix, so $A^\top A = I$ and, for square $A$, $A^\top = A^{-1}$. That is the definition of an orthogonal matrix.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Every orthogonal matrix satisfies the property, e.g. $-I$, the reflection $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ or the rotation $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ (check: $\|(-x_2, x_1)\|^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2$). So $I$ is not the only solution.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Eigenvalues of an orthogonal matrix have modulus $1$ but need not be real. The $90^\circ$ rotation $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ preserves norms, and its characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 + 1$ gives eigenvalues $\pm i$. (The claim does hold when $n = 1$, where $A = \pm 1$, or for symmetric orthogonal matrices, but not ALWAYS.)

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: If $Ax = 0$ then $\|x\| = \|Ax\| = 0$, so $x = 0$. The null space is $\{0\}$ and, by rank–nullity, $\operatorname{rank} A = n$. Equivalently, $\det A = \pm 1 \ne 0$.

solution.shortcut: Norm-preserving square matrix $\iff$ orthogonal ($A^\top A = I$), which gives (A) and, via $\det A = \pm 1$, (D). A single test matrix, the $90^\circ$ rotation $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, preserves norms yet is not $I$ and has eigenvalues $\pm i$, killing (B) and (C) at once.
solution.commonTrap: Selecting (C) from the half-remembered fact "orthogonal matrices have eigenvalues $\pm 1$". The correct statement is $|\lambda| = 1$: only the **real** eigenvalues are forced to be $\pm 1$, and rotations have complex eigenvalues such as $\pm i$. Checking only diagonal examples like $I$, $-I$ or $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)$ hides this.

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.notes: Proof: ||Ax||^2 = ||x||^2 for all x gives x^T(A^T A - I)x = 0 for all x, and since A^T A - I is symmetric this forces A^T A = I, so A is orthogonal (A) and det A = ±1, so A has full rank (D). The sympy part of the check confirms, for a general 2x2 matrix, that the coefficients of ||Ax||^2 - ||x||^2 are exactly the entries of A^T A - I. The numpy part confirms that I, -I, the 90-degree rotation, the reflection diag(1, -1) and a random 5x5 orthogonal matrix all preserve norms and have full rank, so I is not the only solution (B false), and that the rotation has eigenvalues ±i (C false; all eigenvalues have modulus 1). This gives A;D, matching the official key A;D.
